tips.title: Count the atoms to tell them apart
tips.body: Repeating unit has the **same** atoms as the monomer → **addition**. **Fewer** atoms than the monomers together → **condensation**, and the missing atoms are the small molecule lost. This works on monomers you have never seen.

tips.title: Three things every repeating unit needs
tips.body: A **single** bond where the C=C was, a **bond out of each end**, and **brackets with an n**. Missing any one of the three loses a mark, and they take three seconds each to check before you move on.

tips.title: Two groups means condensation
tips.body: One **C=C** points to addition. **Two functional groups** on a monomer — two –OH, or two –COOH — points to condensation, because a chain has to be able to grow at both ends.

tips.title: Poly(ethene), never poly(ethane)
tips.body: The polymer is named from its **monomer**, and only the alkene can polymerise. Ethane is saturated and has no double bond to open, so poly(ethane) does not exist — the vowel is chemistry, not spelling.

tips.title: One water per link
tips.body: In condensation polymerisation a small molecule leaves **each time a link forms**. A diol joining a diacid at both ends makes two ester links, so **two** water molecules go per repeating unit.

steps.title: Many small molecules, one very large one
steps.body:
A **polymer** is a very large molecule made by joining many small molecules together. The small molecules are called **monomers**.

**Addition polymerisation** is the simpler of the two kinds, and it uses **alkenes**. Because alkenes have a **C=C double bond**, they can add to each other: the double bond in each monomer opens, and the freed bonds join to the molecules on either side.

The defining feature is in the name:

$$\textbf{In addition polymerisation, no other molecule is formed.}$$

Everything that was in the monomers ends up in the polymer. So the **repeating unit has exactly the same atoms as the monomer** — the same carbons and the same hydrogens, just joined differently.

Poly(ethene) is made from **ethene**, poly(propene) from **propene**. The name is simply *poly* plus the monomer's name in brackets, and the bracket tells you what the repeating unit is made from.

steps.title: Condensation polymerisation
steps.body:
This section is **Higher tier only**.

**Condensation polymerisation** works differently, and the difference is worth stating precisely. It involves monomers with **two functional groups** — one at each end — and when they join, a **small molecule is lost**, usually **water**. That loss is what the word *condensation* refers to.

The simplest case uses **two different monomers**, each with **two of the same functional group**:

- a **diol** — two –OH groups, such as **ethanediol**
- a **dicarboxylic acid** — two –COOH groups, such as **hexanedioic acid**

An –OH on one reacts with a –COOH on the other, forming an **ester link** and releasing a **water** molecule. Because each monomer has a second group free at its other end, the chain keeps growing from both ends. The polymer formed is a **polyester**.

So two things are produced, not one: the **polyester** and **water**. Contrast that with addition polymerisation, where the polymer is the only product.

How many water molecules? One for **each link formed**. Joining a diol to a diacid at both ends forms two links, so **two water molecules** per repeating unit.

steps.title: Why polymer properties differ
steps.body:
Polymers are useful because their properties can be very different from the monomers they are made from, and from each other.

Poly(ethene) is a **flexible solid**, while the ethene it is made from is a **gas**. The reason is size: a polymer molecule is enormous, so the **intermolecular forces** between chains add up over a huge length and become strong enough to hold the material together as a solid.

That also explains why polymers do **not** have a sharp melting point. The chains are not all the same length, so different parts of the material need different amounts of energy to separate — the material softens over a range instead.

**Durability cuts both ways.** Addition polymers such as poly(ethene) are **unreactive**, which is exactly what makes them useful for packaging — and exactly what makes them a problem in landfill, where they are **not biodegradable** and persist for a very long time.

Polyesters, made by condensation, contain **ester links** that can be broken down again, which is one reason some are easier to recycle or to break down than addition polymers.

steps.title: Going deeper: telling the two apart, and drawing well
steps.body:
**The one-line test.** Count the atoms.

- Repeating unit has the **same atoms** as the monomer → **addition**.
- Repeating unit has **fewer** atoms than the monomers together → **condensation**, and the missing atoms are the small molecule lost.

This works even on a monomer you have never seen, which is why it is worth having instead of a memorised list.

**The other test: look for the functional groups.** An addition monomer needs **one C=C**. A condensation monomer needs **two functional groups**, one at each end — that is what lets the chain grow in both directions. A molecule with only one functional group can join to one neighbour and then stop, so it cannot form a polymer at all.

**Drawing marks are lost in three places:**

1. **Leaving the double bond in.** The whole point is that it opened. Change it to a single bond.
2. **Forgetting the bonds out of the ends.** Without them you have drawn a molecule, not a repeating unit. The chain has to continue.
3. **Forgetting the brackets and the n.** They say *this repeats many times*, and without them the drawing claims something different.

**Naming.** Poly(ethene) is named from **ethene**, the monomer — not from ethane, which has no double bond and cannot polymerise. Getting that vowel wrong changes the chemistry, not just the spelling.

**Why unreactive means both useful and a problem.** Addition polymers have no double bonds left, so there is nothing for other substances to react with. That is why they resist water, acids and air, and why they last in landfill. The same property is an advantage in a food container and a disadvantage the moment it is thrown away — and a question asking you to evaluate a polymer is usually asking you to notice that it is one property, not two.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A **polymer** is a very large molecule made from many small **monomers**.
- **Addition polymerisation** uses **alkenes**: the **C=C opens** and the monomers join.
- **No other molecule is formed**, so the **repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer**.
- Poly(ethene) comes from **ethene**, poly(propene) from **propene**.
- To draw a repeating unit: open the double bond, add a **bond out of each end**, and put **brackets with an n** round it.
- **Higher tier — condensation polymerisation**: monomers with **two functional groups** join, losing a **small molecule**, usually **water**.
- A **diol** and a **dicarboxylic acid** give a **polyester**, joined by **ester links**.
- **Two products**, not one: the polymer **and** water — one water per link formed.
- To tell them apart, **count the atoms**: the same means addition, fewer means condensation.
- Polymers are **solids** although their monomers may be gases, because the molecules are very large and the forces between them add up.
- Addition polymers are **unreactive**, which makes them useful and also makes them persist in landfill.

questions.prompt: Describe addition polymerisation, using ethene as your example. Explain how the repeating unit is drawn from the monomer, and state how the atoms in the repeating unit compare with those in the monomer.
questions.solution: In addition polymerisation many small alkene molecules, called monomers, join together to form one very large molecule called a polymer. Ethene has a carbon to carbon double bond. During polymerisation this double bond opens, and the freed bonds are used to join each monomer to the ones on either side of it, so that the carbons form a long chain. To draw the repeating unit, first draw the monomer with every bond shown as a line, then change the double bond into a single bond, then draw a bond coming out of each end of the unit to show that the chain continues in both directions, and finally put square brackets around the unit with the letter n outside at the bottom right to show that the unit repeats very many times. Because no other molecule is formed in the reaction, the repeating unit contains exactly the same atoms as the monomer, in this case two carbon atoms and four hydrogen atoms.

questions.modelAnswer:
**What happens.** Many small **alkene** monomers join to form one very large molecule. In ethene, the **C=C double bond opens**, and the freed bonds join each monomer to its neighbours, building a long carbon chain.

**Drawing the repeating unit**, in four steps:

1. Draw the **monomer**, every bond as a line.
2. Change the **double bond to a single bond** — it opened.
3. Draw a **bond out of each end**, showing the chain continues both ways.
4. Put **square brackets** round it with **n** outside, bottom right.

**The atoms.** Because **no other molecule is formed**, the repeating unit has **exactly the same atoms as the monomer**: for ethene, two carbons and four hydrogens.

That last point is also a check on your own drawing. If your repeating unit has gained or lost an atom, one of the four steps went wrong.

questions.prompt: Compare addition polymerisation with condensation polymerisation. Refer to the monomers used, the functional groups needed, what is produced, and how the atoms in the repeating unit compare with those in the monomers.
questions.solution: In addition polymerisation the monomers are alkenes, each containing one carbon to carbon double bond. The double bonds open and the monomers join together, and no other molecule is formed, so the polymer is the only product. This means the repeating unit contains exactly the same atoms as the monomer. Poly ethene made from ethene is an example. In condensation polymerisation each monomer must have two functional groups, one at each end, so that the chain can grow in both directions. Commonly two different monomers are used, such as a diol with two O H groups and a dicarboxylic acid with two C O O H groups. When they join, an ester link is formed and a small molecule, usually water, is lost, so there are two products rather than one. The polymer formed is a polyester. Because water is lost each time a link forms, the repeating unit contains fewer atoms than the monomers did between them, and the missing atoms are exactly those of the water molecules released.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Addition polymerisation.**

- **Monomers:** alkenes, each with one **C=C**.
- **What happens:** the double bonds open and the monomers join.
- **Products:** the polymer **only** — nothing else is formed.
- **Atoms:** the repeating unit has **exactly the same atoms** as the monomer.
- **Example:** poly(ethene) from ethene.

**Condensation polymerisation.**

- **Monomers:** each needs **two functional groups**, one at each end, so the chain can grow both ways. Commonly two different monomers — a **diol** (two –OH) and a **dicarboxylic acid** (two –COOH).
- **What happens:** an –OH reacts with a –COOH to form an **ester link**, releasing a **water** molecule.
- **Products:** **two** — the **polyester** and **water**.
- **Atoms:** the repeating unit has **fewer** atoms than the monomers had between them, and what is missing is exactly the water released.

**The one-line test.** Count the atoms in the repeating unit against the monomers. Same means addition; fewer means condensation, and the difference names the small molecule lost. That test works on monomers you have never seen before.

examTechnique.body:
Start by looking at the monomer's functional groups: one C=C means addition, two groups means condensation.

When drawing a repeating unit, work through the four steps in order and then check all three features are there: single bond, bonds out of both ends, brackets with an n.

Count the atoms in your repeating unit against the monomer. For addition they must match exactly, and that check will catch most drawing errors.

For condensation, name the link formed as well as the small molecule lost, and say how many water molecules leave and why.

When asked to compare the two, use the same four headings for each: monomers, functional groups, products, and atoms in the repeating unit. That structure makes sure nothing is left out.

Give the polymer its monomer's name, with the alkene spelling.
examinerErrors: Leaving the double bond in the repeating unit.
Drawing a repeating unit with no bonds coming out of the ends.
Forgetting the brackets and the n.
Saying water is formed in addition polymerisation, where nothing else is formed.
Saying only one water molecule is lost when two links are formed.
Giving a condensation monomer only one functional group.
Saying the repeating unit is the same as the monomer for a condensation polymer.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer identifies the kind of polymerisation from the functional groups before doing anything else, and can also work it out backwards by counting atoms when only formulae are given. Its repeating units always have the three features, because it checks them rather than remembering them. It explains condensation in terms of two functional groups allowing growth at both ends, which is the reason behind the rule rather than the rule itself. It counts one small molecule per link rather than one per reaction. And it treats the unreactivity of addition polymers as a single property with two consequences — useful in packaging, persistent in landfill — rather than as two separate facts.
